one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens his Jan 3, 2016 column with a self-effacing tribute to the late Letty Jimenez-Magsanoc, Inquirer editor-in-chief -- 'fearless, intuitive and spiritual,' and refusing any attention to herself, preferring to ascribe her success to her people and readers. Picking up the second of two pre-holiday columns, he then surveys civilizational change through personal autobiography. Readers can access him via print bought from newsboys (as he once was, racing competitors in Sampaloc and shouting 'Manila Times, Chronicle, Herald' -- the Inquirer was not yet born -- along España Street, peddling leftover copies to jeepney passengers stopped at red lights), or via digital edition on tablets and smartphones, or via Inquirer.net, or via social media. Newspapers retain value beyond breaking news for in-depth opinions and features. Digital cameras killed Kodak; smartphone apps are now killing cameras and will soon replace movie houses, TV, passports, credit cards, keys, even cash. Land lines have been overtaken by mobile; long-distance has been obliterated by Magic Jack, Viber, and Skype; SMS is giving way to iMessaging. In medicine and science, he testifies personally: 2008 cataract laser surgery restored his 20/20 vision (he still wears eyeglasses occasionally because his wife thinks it more becoming a retired chief justice); prostate biopsy and kidney/gall stone surgery have become minimally invasive; IVF enables barren couples to enjoy parenthood; artificial limbs allow the handicapped to walk; biotechnological breakthroughs presage lab-grown body parts. The Paris Agreement is ambitious but a huge milestone, uniting heretofore ideological incompatibles into a single voice to hold the rise of earth's temperature to 1.5°C by 2100. The Hubble telescope reveals our sun as just one grain of sand on the kilometric beaches of the universe; European astroscientists recently piggybacked the Rosetta spacecraft on a comet to investigate how the universe was born. On globalization, the WTO ushered in the era of liberalization, privatization, and deregulation two decades ago -- but many Filipinos still pine for 'Filipino First.' Whether we like it or not, we have to face free trade and open competition; isolationism has no more place. Asean formally integrated three days ago. China embraced capitalism while keeping its communist political system; only North Korea has refused globalization, plunging its people to abject poverty opposite South Korea's prosperity. Engineering, accounting, medicine, and nursing have already accepted reciprocal globalization; it is time for lawyers to allow foreign counterparts to practice here, provided Philippine lawyers are reciprocally allowed to practice abroad. The world is changing fast and so must we, lest we be left behind in ignorance, regression, and destitution. Many businessmen and professionals have proven Filipinos can hold their own against the best of the world. The Filipino can! He closes circularly: 'In facing the new year, let's be like Letty: fearless, intuitive and spiritual.'
